---
title: "Univariate models"
subtitle: "Stationarity, ARMA, SARIMA, ETS, Holt-Winters and a seasonal naive benchmark"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/setup.R")

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tseries)  # adf.test, jarque.bera.test
  library(urca)     # ur.kpss
  library(uroot)    # hegy.test
  library(lmtest)   # coeftest
  library(FinTS)    # ArchTest
})

# Format a p-value for the text, including the relation sign ("= 0.0100", "< 2.2e-16")
fmt_p <- function(p) {
  if (p < 2.2e-16) return("< 2.2e-16")
  if (p < 0.001) return(paste("=", format(p, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE)))
  paste("=", sprintf("%.4f", p))
}

# KPSS statistics with the 5% critical value
kpss_table <- function(x) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("tau", "mu"), function(type) {
    t <- ur.kpss(x, type = type)
    data.frame(
      Specification = if (type == "tau") "Trend (tau)" else "Constant (mu)",
      Statistic = round(t@teststat, 4),
      `Critical value 5%` = t@cval[, "5pct"],
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }))
}

# ADF p-values for several lag orders (tseries reports p-values within [0.01, 0.99])
adf_lags <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 24)
adf_table <- function(x) {
  data.frame(
    Lag = adf_lags,
    `p-value` = sapply(adf_lags, function(k) suppressWarnings(adf.test(x, k = k)$p.value)),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

# HEGY statistics and p-values by frequency. The test regression includes a
# constant, a linear trend and monthly dummies (deterministic = c(1, 1, 1)), and
# the number of augmentation lags is chosen by BIC so that its residuals are not
# autocorrelated.
hegy_table <- function(x) {
  h <- hegy.test(x, deterministic = c(1, 1, 1), lag.method = "BIC", maxlag = 12)
  data.frame(
    Statistic = names(h$statistics),
    Value = round(h$statistics, 3),
    `p-value` = round(h$pvalues, 4),
    check.names = FALSE,
    row.names = NULL
  )
}
```

The series is the US Industrial Production Total Index (IPB50001N, 2017 = 100,
not seasonally adjusted), monthly from January 1990 to April 2025
(`r length(ip_ts)` observations).

## Visual analysis

```{r}
#| label: fig-ip-level
#| fig-cap: "US industrial production, total index"
autoplot(ip_ts) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)")
```

The series has a strong upward trend between 1990 and 2008, so its mean is not
constant, which is a first sign of non-stationarity. Two major shocks stand out:
the collapse during the 2008–2009 financial crisis and the very sharp but
short-lived drop during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The trend and the level
shifts call for formal unit root testing.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ip-acf
#| fig-cap: "Series, ACF and PACF in levels"
ggtsdisplay(ip_ts)
```

The ACF decays very slowly and almost linearly, staying far above the
significance bands: the classic pattern of a non-stationary (unit root) process.
The PACF has a large spike at lag 1 and significant spikes at the seasonal lags
12 and 24. Visually, the series needs both a regular difference (for the trend)
and a seasonal difference at lag 12.

```{r}
#| label: fig-subseries
#| fig-cap: "Seasonal subseries: one panel per month, blue line = monthly mean"
ggsubseriesplot(ip_ts) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Index (2017 = 100)")
```

The monthly means differ: June and August have the highest average production,
while April and July are lower. Unequal monthly means are visual evidence of a
seasonal component, which motivates the HEGY test for seasonal unit roots.

## Stationarity tests in levels

**KPSS** (null hypothesis: the series is stationary):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-kpss-level
#| tbl-cap: "KPSS test, series in levels"
kpss_level <- kpss_table(ip_ts)
kpss_level
```

In both specifications the statistic is far above the 5% critical value, so
stationarity is rejected: the original series is non-stationary.

**ADF** (null hypothesis: unit root) for several lag orders, and
**Phillips-Perron**:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-adf-level
#| tbl-cap: "ADF p-values by lag order, series in levels"
adf_level <- adf_table(ip_ts)
pp_level <- PP.test(ip_ts)
adf_level
```

All ADF p-values are well above 0.05, so the unit root cannot be rejected. The
Phillips-Perron test gives p `r fmt_p(pp_level$p.value)` and leads to the same
conclusion. KPSS, ADF and PP all agree that the series is non-stationary in levels.

## Seasonality test (HEGY)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hegy-level
#| tbl-cap: "HEGY test on the log series (constant, trend and monthly dummies; lags chosen by BIC)"
hegy_level <- hegy_table(log(ip_ts))
hegy_level
```

The HEGY test checks for unit roots at the zero frequency (`t_1`, an ordinary
stochastic trend) and at each seasonal frequency (`t_2` and the F-statistics).
Because the series has a trend and a seasonal pattern, the test regression
includes a constant, a trend and monthly dummies.

- For `t_1`, p
  `r fmt_p(hegy_level[["p-value"]][hegy_level$Statistic == "t_1"])` (> 0.05):
  the zero-frequency unit root is not rejected, so the series needs a regular
  (first) difference.
- At all seasonal frequencies the p-values are below
  `r ceiling(100 * max(hegy_level[["p-value"]][hegy_level$Statistic != "t_1"])) / 100`:
  seasonal unit roots are rejected. The seasonal pattern is **deterministic**
  (a stable pattern by month), not stochastic.

Strictly, this points to a first difference with monthly dummies rather than a
seasonal difference. The analysis below follows the usual SARIMA route with
both a log transformation and a seasonal difference at lag 12, which is also
what `auto.arima()` selects. Seasonally differencing a series without seasonal
unit roots can over-difference it; this would show up as a seasonal MA
coefficient close to −1 in the SARIMA model, which is checked below.

## Transformations

```{r}
#| label: transform
ip_log <- log(ip_ts)
ip_seasonal_diff <- diff(ip_log, lag = 12)
ip_stationary <- diff(ip_seasonal_diff)
```

After the log transformation, the seasonal difference and a first difference,
the unit root tests are repeated on the final series:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-tests-stationary
#| tbl-cap: "KPSS and ADF tests, stationary series"
kpss_table(ip_stationary)
adf_stationary <- adf_table(ip_stationary)
pp_stationary <- PP.test(ip_stationary)
adf_stationary
```

The KPSS statistics are now far below their 5% critical values, so
stationarity is not rejected. All ADF p-values are 0.01, the smallest value
`adf.test()` reports (the true
p-value is lower), and Phillips-Perron gives p `r fmt_p(pp_stationary$p.value)`.
The unit root is strongly rejected: the transformed series is stationary.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stationary
#| fig-cap: "Stationary series: log, seasonal difference and first difference"
autoplot(ip_stationary) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL)
```

The transformed series no longer trends and fluctuates around zero. Higher
volatility in 2008 and 2020 reflects the crisis episodes, but mean reversion is
now clear.

## Train / test split

```{r}
#| label: split
n_total <- length(ip_ts)
n_train <- floor(0.75 * n_total)

ip_train <- window(ip_ts, end = time(ip_ts)[n_train])
ip_test <- window(ip_ts, start = time(ip_ts)[n_train + 1])
ip_train_log <- window(ip_log, end = time(ip_log)[n_train])

h <- length(ip_test)
```

The first 75% of the sample (`r n_train` months, to
`r format(zoo::as.yearmon(time(ip_train)[n_train]))`) is used to estimate the
models; the last `r h` months (`r format(zoo::as.yearmon(time(ip_test)[1]))`
to `r format(zoo::as.yearmon(time(ip_test)[h]))`) are kept for out-of-sample
evaluation. The forecast horizon `h` equals the length of the test set, so RMSE,
MAE and MAPE can be computed on it.

## ARMA models on the stationary series

```{r}
#| label: fig-arma-acf
#| fig-cap: "Training part of the stationary series, ACF and PACF"
# Same end date as the training set (June 2016), so no test months are used
ip_stationary_train <- window(ip_stationary, end = time(ip_train)[n_train])

ggtsdisplay(ip_stationary_train)
```

Short lags (1–4) are significant in both the ACF and PACF, which points to
short-run AR and MA components. There are also large negative spikes at the
seasonal lags 12 and 24, so a non-seasonal ARMA model will struggle to remove
the autocorrelation at long lags. This is why several models are estimated and
why SARIMA follows.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-arma
#| tbl-cap: "Candidate ARMA models on the stationary training series"
arma_orders <- list(c(1, 0, 0), c(0, 0, 1), c(1, 0, 1), c(1, 0, 2), c(2, 0, 1))
arma_models <- lapply(arma_orders, function(o) Arima(ip_stationary_train, order = o))
arma_auto <- auto.arima(ip_stationary_train, seasonal = FALSE)

arma_compare <- data.frame(
  Model = c(sapply(arma_orders, function(o) sprintf("ARMA(%d,%d)", o[1], o[3])), "auto.arima"),
  Specification = c(sapply(arma_models, function(m) as.character(m)), as.character(arma_auto)),
  AIC = round(c(sapply(arma_models, AIC), AIC(arma_auto)), 2),
  BIC = round(c(sapply(arma_models, BIC), BIC(arma_auto)), 2)
)
arma_compare

coeftest(arma_auto)
```

`auto.arima()` selects `r as.character(arma_auto)` with AIC = `r round(arma_auto$aic, 2)`
and BIC = `r round(arma_auto$bic, 2)`, the lowest values among the candidates.
The coefficients ar2, ma2 and ma3 are significant at 1% and ma1 at 5%; ar1 is
not significant on its own but is kept to preserve the AR(2) structure.

```{r}
#| label: fig-arma-resid
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics, ARMA model"
arma_lb <- checkresiduals(arma_auto)
```

The Ljung-Box test gives p `r fmt_p(arma_lb$p.value)` (< 0.05), so the null
hypothesis of independent residuals is rejected: the residuals are not white
noise. The ACF confirms remaining autocorrelation at the seasonal lags 12 and 24.
A non-seasonal ARMA model cannot capture the full dynamics of the series, which
justifies moving to SARIMA.

## SARIMA

```{r}
#| label: sarima
sarima_final <- auto.arima(
  ip_train_log,
  seasonal = TRUE,
  stepwise = FALSE,
  approximation = FALSE
)
sarima_final
coeftest(sarima_final)
```

`auto.arima()` selects `r as.character(sarima_final)` on the log of the training
data, with both a regular (d = 1) and a seasonal (D = 1) difference, as suggested
by the analysis above. The fit improves considerably: AIC falls to
`r round(sarima_final$aic, 2)` (from `r round(arma_auto$aic, 2)` for ARMA; both
models are fitted to the same differenced training observations, so their AIC
values are comparable).
ar2, ar3 and the seasonal MA term sma1 are highly significant (p < 0.01); ar1 is
kept for the consistency of the AR(3) structure. The seasonal MA coefficient,
`r round(coef(sarima_final)["sma1"], 2)`, is well away from −1, so there is no
sign that the seasonal difference over-differences the series.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sarima-resid
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics, SARIMA model"
sarima_lb <- checkresiduals(sarima_final)
```

The Ljung-Box test gives p `r fmt_p(sarima_lb$p.value)` (> 0.05): the residuals
show no autocorrelation and behave like white noise. The seasonal MA term
removed the correlation at lags 12 and 24, and the histogram is roughly
symmetric.

### Further residual tests

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sarima-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Ljung-Box and ARCH tests on the SARIMA residuals"
sarima_resid <- residuals(sarima_final)

lb_lags <- c(1:5, 8, 12, 24)
sarima_lb_table <- data.frame(
  Lag = lb_lags,
  `Ljung-Box p-value` = sapply(lb_lags, function(l) {
    Box.test(sarima_resid, lag = l, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value
  }),
  check.names = FALSE
)

arch_lags <- c(1, 2, 4, 8, 12)
sarima_arch_table <- data.frame(
  Lag = arch_lags,
  `ARCH p-value` = sapply(arch_lags, function(l) ArchTest(sarima_resid, lags = l)$p.value),
  check.names = FALSE
)

sarima_jb <- jarque.bera.test(sarima_resid)

sarima_lb_table
sarima_arch_table
```

1. **Autocorrelation (Ljung-Box):** all p-values are high (minimum
   `r round(min(sarima_lb_table[[2]]), 3)`), so the residuals are independent
   and the dynamics have been captured.
2. **Normality (Jarque-Bera):** p `r fmt_p(sarima_jb$p.value)` (< 0.05), so
   normality is rejected. This is explained by turning points and major shocks
   (the 2008 crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 shock).
3. **Heteroscedasticity (ARCH):** p-values below 0.05 show ARCH effects
   (volatility clustering): the error variance is not constant, with larger
   residuals during episodes of macroeconomic instability.

The model is valid for the conditional mean and is used for forecasting.

### SARIMA forecast

```{r}
#| label: fig-sarima-forecast
#| fig-cap: "SARIMA forecast (back-transformed to index levels) against the test data"
# Back-transform to index levels. The same model (same coefficients) is applied
# to the series with lambda = 0, i.e. a log transformation, so forecast()
# returns exp() of the log forecasts: the point forecast is the median of the
# forecast distribution and the interval bounds (quantiles) carry over exactly.
sarima_lvl <- Arima(ip_train, model = sarima_final, lambda = 0)
sarima_real <- forecast(sarima_lvl, h = h)

# For comparison: the bias-adjusted mean forecast
sarima_mean <- forecast(Arima(ip_train, model = sarima_final, lambda = 0, biasadj = TRUE), h = h)
sarima_mean_rmse <- accuracy(sarima_mean$mean, ip_test)[1, "RMSE"]

autoplot(sarima_real) +
  autolayer(ip_test, series = "Test data") +
  labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL)
```

1. The forecasts are made for the log of the index and converted back with
   exp(). This gives the **median** forecast, and the prediction intervals stay
   valid because quantiles are preserved by exp(). The **mean** forecast would
   be higher by roughly half the forecast variance, which grows quickly with the
   horizon: the gap is
   `r round(sarima_mean$mean[12] - sarima_real$mean[12], 2)` index points after
   12 months but `r round(sarima_mean$mean[h] - sarima_real$mean[h], 1)` after
   `r h` months, and the RMSE on the test period would be
   `r round(sarima_mean_rmse, 2)` instead of
   `r round(accuracy(sarima_real$mean, ip_test)[1, "RMSE"], 2)`. The median is
   used as the point forecast.
2. The forecast (blue) follows the centre of the test data (2016–2025) closely
   from this single origin; the rolling-origin evaluation below gives a more
   complete picture of out-of-sample performance.
3. The 2020 COVID-19 shock appears as a large exogenous deviation; the data
   later return to the forecast path.
4. The uncertainty fan widens asymmetrically, as expected for long-horizon
   forecasts on a log scale.

## Exponential smoothing (ETS)

```{r}
#| label: ets
ets_auto <- ets(ip_train, model = "ZZZ")
ets_auto
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ets-resid
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics, ETS model"
ets_lb <- checkresiduals(ets_auto)
```

The automatic selection gives `r ets_auto$method`: multiplicative errors, an
additive damped trend (φ = `r round(ets_auto$par["phi"], 4)`) and multiplicative
seasonality. The Ljung-Box test gives p `r fmt_p(ets_lb$p.value)` (< 0.05),
so the residuals are not white noise, and the ACF shows remaining
autocorrelation at short and seasonal lags (12, 24). In-sample, ETS leaves
information in the residuals and is inferior to SARIMA in this respect,
although out of sample the two models perform similarly (see the
rolling-origin evaluation).

```{r}
#| label: fig-ets-forecast
#| fig-cap: "ETS forecast against the test data"
ets_forecast <- forecast(ets_auto, h = h)

autoplot(ets_forecast) +
  autolayer(ip_test, series = "Test data") +
  labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL)
```

1. ETS reproduces the seasonal pattern but slightly underestimates the level
   over the test period.
2. The damped trend stabilises the central path and prevents unrealistic
   long-run growth.
3. The prediction intervals widen more slowly than for SARIMA: at the end of
   the test period (`r format(zoo::as.yearmon(time(ets_forecast$mean)[h]))`)
   the upper 95% bound is `r round(ets_forecast$upper[h, "95%"], 1)`, compared
   with `r round(sarima_real$upper[h, "95%"], 1)` for SARIMA.

## Holt-Winters

```{r}
#| label: hw
hw_add <- hw(ip_train, seasonal = "additive", h = h)
hw_mult <- hw(ip_train, seasonal = "multiplicative", h = h)

hw_lo95 <- hw_add$lower[, "95%"]
hw_first_negative <- time(hw_lo95)[which(hw_lo95 < 0)[1]]

data.frame(
  Model = c("Additive", "Multiplicative"),
  AIC = round(c(hw_add$model$aic, hw_mult$model$aic), 2),
  `RMSE (train)` = round(c(accuracy(hw_add)[, "RMSE"], accuracy(hw_mult)[, "RMSE"]), 4),
  alpha = round(c(hw_add$model$par["alpha"], hw_mult$model$par["alpha"]), 4),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

1. The additive model fits better in-sample than the multiplicative one, with a
   lower AIC and a lower training RMSE.
2. α = `r round(hw_add$model$par["alpha"], 4)` in the additive model means the
   level reacts strongly to the most recent shocks.
3. Limitation: in the forecast of the additive model over the test period, the
   lower 95% bound falls below zero from
   `r format(zoo::as.yearmon(hw_first_negative))`. This shows a weakness of
   classic additive structures on series in levels, compared with log-SARIMA.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hw-resid
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics, additive Holt-Winters"
hw_lb <- checkresiduals(hw_add)
```

The Ljung-Box test gives p `r fmt_p(hw_lb$p.value)` (< 0.05): the residuals are
not white noise, with large dependencies at the seasonal lags (12, 24, 36).
Holt-Winters makes the seasonal component too rigid and does not remove the
seasonal memory of the index; on in-sample residual diagnostics it is inferior
to SARIMA.

## Seasonal naive benchmark

```{r}
#| label: fig-snaive
#| fig-cap: "Seasonal naive forecast against the test data"
naive_model <- snaive(ip_train, h = h)

autoplot(naive_model) +
  autolayer(ip_test, series = "Test data") +
  labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL)
```

The seasonal naive forecast repeats the last observed seasonal cycle with a flat
trend. It captures the monthly pattern but cannot adapt to changes in the trend,
and its intervals are wide. It is the basic benchmark that more complex models
must beat.

## Model comparison

Each model was estimated on the training data only and forecasts the `r h`
months of the test period, which are compared with the actual values.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Forecast accuracy on the test set (Jul 2016 to Apr 2025)"
sarima_trim <- sarima_real$mean[1:h]
ets_trim <- ets_forecast$mean[1:h]
hw_trim <- hw_add$mean[1:h]
naive_trim <- naive_model$mean[1:h]

acc_table <- rbind(
  SARIMA = accuracy(sarima_trim, ip_test)[1, ],
  ETS = accuracy(ets_trim, ip_test)[1, ],
  HOLT_WINTERS = accuracy(hw_trim, ip_test)[1, ],
  SNAIVE = accuracy(naive_trim, ip_test)[1, ]
)

round(acc_table, 4)
```

1. SARIMA has the smallest errors: RMSE = `r round(acc_table["SARIMA", "RMSE"], 4)`
   and MAPE = `r round(acc_table["SARIMA", "MAPE"], 2)`%.
2. ETS (MAPE = `r round(acc_table["ETS", "MAPE"], 2)`%) and Holt-Winters
   (MAPE = `r round(acc_table["HOLT_WINTERS", "MAPE"], 2)`%) systematically
   underestimate the test data.
3. SARIMA also beats the seasonal naive benchmark
   (MAPE = `r round(acc_table["SNAIVE", "MAPE"], 2)`%).

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Forecasts over the test period"
to_test_ts <- function(x) ts(x[1:h], start = start(ip_test), frequency = 12)

autoplot(ip_ts, series = "Actual") +
  autolayer(to_test_ts(sarima_real$mean), series = "SARIMA", linewidth = 1) +
  autolayer(to_test_ts(ets_forecast$mean), series = "ETS", linewidth = 1) +
  autolayer(to_test_ts(hw_add$mean), series = "Holt-Winters", linewidth = 1) +
  autolayer(to_test_ts(naive_model$mean), series = "Seasonal naive", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL)
```

The chart is consistent with the accuracy table. SARIMA follows the level and
the fluctuations of the actual series closely, around 100 index points. ETS and
Holt-Winters drift downwards and underestimate the series, which explains their
large errors. The seasonal naive forecast does reasonably well thanks to its
flat trend but does not adapt to the dynamics of the series.

This comparison rests on a **single forecast origin** (June 2016): each error
is a forecast from 1 to `r h` months ahead, and the result depends heavily on
where the trend of each model happened to point in mid-2016. The errors are
also strongly autocorrelated (first-order autocorrelation of
`r round(acc_table["SARIMA", "ACF1"], 2)` for SARIMA), so a Diebold-Mariano test
that treats them as independent one-step errors would overstate the
significance of the differences. A rolling-origin evaluation gives a more
reliable comparison.

## Rolling-origin evaluation

Here the models are re-estimated every month of the test period on all data
available up to that month (an expanding window) and forecast the next 1 to 12
months, as an analyst updating the forecast every month would do. Each model
keeps the specification selected on the training data; only its parameters are
re-estimated. SARIMA forecasts are medians, as above.

```{r}
#| label: rolling-cv
max_h <- 12
sarima_order <- arimaorder(sarima_final)

# Forecast functions with the specifications chosen on the training data
ets_spec <- ets_auto$components  # error, trend, season, damped
forecast_functions <- list(
  SARIMA = function(x, h) {
    forecast(Arima(x, order = sarima_order[c("p", "d", "q")],
                   seasonal = sarima_order[c("P", "D", "Q")], lambda = 0), h = h)
  },
  ETS = function(x, h) {
    forecast(ets(x, model = paste0(ets_spec[1], ets_spec[2], ets_spec[3]),
                 damped = as.logical(ets_spec[4])), h = h)
  },
  `Holt-Winters` = function(x, h) hw(x, seasonal = "additive", h = h),
  `Seasonal naive` = function(x, h) snaive(x, h = h)
)

# Row t, column k = error of the k-step forecast made with data up to month t.
# The first origin is the end of the training sample (June 2016).
cv_errors <- lapply(forecast_functions, function(f) {
  tsCV(ip_ts, f, h = max_h, initial = n_train - 1)
})

# Actual value and target date of each k-step forecast, aligned with cv_errors
n_obs <- length(ip_ts)
target_value <- function(k) c(as.numeric(ip_ts)[-(1:k)], rep(NA, k))
target_time <- function(k) c(as.numeric(time(ip_ts))[-(1:k)], rep(NA, k))

cv_accuracy <- function(k, exclude_covid = FALSE) {
  keep <- !is.na(target_value(k))
  if (exclude_covid) {
    keep <- keep & !(target_time(k) >= 2020 + 2 / 12 & target_time(k) < 2021.5)
  }
  t(sapply(cv_errors, function(E) {
    e <- E[, k]
    ok <- keep & !is.na(e)
    c(Forecasts = sum(ok),
      RMSE = sqrt(mean(e[ok]^2)),
      MAE = mean(abs(e[ok])),
      `MAPE (%)` = 100 * mean(abs(e[ok] / target_value(k)[ok])))
  }))
}

cv_1 <- cv_accuracy(1)
cv_12 <- cv_accuracy(12)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cv-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Rolling-origin accuracy, 1 and 12 months ahead"
cv_table <- rbind(
  data.frame(Horizon = "1 month", Model = rownames(cv_1), round(cv_1, 3), check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(Horizon = "12 months", Model = rownames(cv_12), round(cv_12, 3), check.names = FALSE)
)
rownames(cv_table) <- NULL
cv_table
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cv-rmse
#| fig-cap: "Rolling-origin RMSE by forecast horizon"
cv_rmse <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cv_errors), function(m) {
  data.frame(
    Model = m,
    Horizon = 1:max_h,
    RMSE = sapply(1:max_h, function(k) {
      e <- cv_errors[[m]][, k]
      sqrt(mean(e[!is.na(e) & !is.na(target_value(k))]^2))
    })
  )
}))

ggplot(cv_rmse, aes(Horizon, RMSE, colour = Model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:max_h) +
  labs(x = "Months ahead", y = "RMSE (index points)", colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: cv-crossover
rmse_of <- function(m) cv_rmse$RMSE[cv_rmse$Model == m]
sarima_last_better <- max(which(rmse_of("SARIMA") < rmse_of("Seasonal naive")))
ets_last_better <- max(which(rmse_of("ETS") < rmse_of("Seasonal naive")))
```

The errors of the statistical models grow quickly with the horizon, while the
seasonal naive error stays almost flat. The seasonal naive forecast has a lower
RMSE than SARIMA from `r sarima_last_better + 1` months ahead and than ETS from
`r ets_last_better + 1` months ahead. Whether these differences are
statistically significant is tested below.

The 2020 pandemic produces a few very large errors that dominate the RMSE. As
a robustness check, the table below excludes forecasts whose target month falls
between March 2020 and June 2021:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cv-no-covid
#| tbl-cap: "Rolling-origin accuracy excluding targets from March 2020 to June 2021"
cv_1_nc <- cv_accuracy(1, exclude_covid = TRUE)
cv_12_nc <- cv_accuracy(12, exclude_covid = TRUE)
cv_table_nc <- rbind(
  data.frame(Horizon = "1 month", Model = rownames(cv_1_nc), round(cv_1_nc, 3), check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(Horizon = "12 months", Model = rownames(cv_12_nc), round(cv_12_nc, 3), check.names = FALSE)
)
rownames(cv_table_nc) <- NULL
cv_table_nc
```

### Diebold-Mariano tests

The Diebold-Mariano test compares the squared errors of SARIMA with those of
each other model on the same forecast origins. The null hypothesis is equal
accuracy; a negative statistic means SARIMA has smaller errors. For 12-month
forecasts, consecutive errors overlap, and `h = 12` makes the test account for
the resulting autocorrelation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dm
#| tbl-cap: "Diebold-Mariano tests on rolling-origin errors (SARIMA vs each model)"
dm_rows <- list()
for (k in c(1, max_h)) {
  for (m in setdiff(names(cv_errors), "SARIMA")) {
    a <- cv_errors$SARIMA[, k]
    b <- cv_errors[[m]][, k]
    ok <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)
    test <- dm.test(a[ok], b[ok], alternative = "two.sided", h = k, power = 2)
    dm_rows[[length(dm_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      Horizon = paste(k, if (k == 1) "month" else "months"),
      Comparison = paste("SARIMA vs", m),
      `DM statistic` = round(unname(test$statistic), 3),
      `p-value` = signif(test$p.value, 3),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }
}
dm_table <- do.call(rbind, dm_rows)
rownames(dm_table) <- NULL

# Display copy with readable p-values
dm_display <- dm_table
dm_display[["p-value"]] <- ifelse(
  dm_table[["p-value"]] < 0.001,
  format(dm_table[["p-value"]], digits = 3, scientific = TRUE),
  sprintf("%.3f", dm_table[["p-value"]])
)
dm_display
```

```{r}
#| label: dm-values
dm_p <- function(horizon, model) {
  dm_table[["p-value"]][dm_table$Horizon == horizon & dm_table$Comparison == paste("SARIMA vs", model)]
}
```

The next table compares each statistical model with the seasonal naive
benchmark at every horizon from 1 to 12 months.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dm-naive
#| tbl-cap: "Diebold-Mariano p-values, each model vs the seasonal naive benchmark, by horizon"
naive_dm <- data.frame(Horizon = 1:max_h)
for (m in c("SARIMA", "ETS", "Holt-Winters")) {
  naive_dm[[m]] <- sapply(1:max_h, function(k) {
    a <- cv_errors[[m]][, k]
    b <- cv_errors[["Seasonal naive"]][, k]
    ok <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)
    dm.test(a[ok], b[ok], alternative = "two.sided", h = k, power = 2)$p.value
  })
}
naive_dm_display <- naive_dm
naive_dm_display[, -1] <- round(naive_dm[, -1], 3)
naive_dm_display

naive_p <- as.matrix(naive_dm[, -1])
```

1. **One month ahead**, SARIMA, ETS and Holt-Winters are very close (RMSE of
   `r sprintf("%.2f", cv_1["SARIMA", "RMSE"])` for SARIMA,
   `r sprintf("%.2f", cv_1["ETS", "RMSE"])` for ETS and
   `r sprintf("%.2f", cv_1["Holt-Winters", "RMSE"])` for Holt-Winters), and the
   Diebold-Mariano test does not distinguish SARIMA from ETS (p `r fmt_p(dm_p("1 month", "ETS"))`) or
   Holt-Winters (p `r fmt_p(dm_p("1 month", "Holt-Winters"))`). All three
   significantly beat the seasonal naive benchmark (RMSE
   `r round(cv_1["Seasonal naive", "RMSE"], 2)`; p-values of at most
   `r sprintf("%.3f", max(naive_p[1, ]))`).
2. **From about four months ahead**, the seasonal naive forecast has a lower
   RMSE than the statistical models (twelve months ahead:
   `r round(cv_12["Seasonal naive", "RMSE"], 2)` against
   `r round(cv_12["SARIMA", "RMSE"], 2)` for SARIMA), but the difference is
   **not statistically significant** at any horizon (from three months on, all
   p-values are above `r floor(100 * min(naive_p[3:max_h, ])) / 100`). Two months
   ahead the evidence that the models beat the benchmark is already weak
   (p between `r sprintf("%.2f", min(naive_p[2, ]))` and
   `r sprintf("%.2f", max(naive_p[2, ]))`).
3. Excluding the pandemic months lowers all errors substantially. One month
   ahead the three statistical models remain almost tied, and twelve months
   ahead the seasonal naive forecast is still the most accurate.

The rolling-origin evaluation does **not** confirm the large advantage of
SARIMA seen with a single forecast origin. One month ahead the three
statistical models perform equally well and significantly beat the seasonal
naive benchmark. From about four months ahead the seasonal naive forecast has
lower errors, but the differences are not statistically significant: on this
sample the models add clear value only at the shortest horizon.

## Forecast beyond the sample

The test period is only used to evaluate the models. To forecast the future,
the selected SARIMA specification is re-estimated on the full sample
(January 1990 to April 2025), so the forecast uses all the available data,
including the years after 2016.

```{r}
#| label: sarima-full
sarima_full <- Arima(
  ip_ts,
  order = sarima_order[c("p", "d", "q")],
  seasonal = sarima_order[c("P", "D", "Q")],
  lambda = 0  # log transformation, as for the training model
)
sarima_full
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-future-forecast
#| fig-cap: "SARIMA forecast for May 2025 to April 2028, estimated on the full sample"
h_future <- 36
future <- forecast(sarima_full, h = h_future)  # median forecast in index points

autoplot(future, include = 120) +
  labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-future-forecast
#| tbl-cap: "SARIMA forecast at selected horizons (index points)"
future_steps <- c(6, 12, 24, 36)
data.frame(
  Month = format(zoo::as.yearmon(time(future$mean)[future_steps])),
  `Months ahead` = future_steps,
  Forecast = round(future$mean[future_steps], 1),
  `80% interval` = sprintf("%.1f – %.1f", future$lower[future_steps, "80%"], future$upper[future_steps, "80%"]),
  `95% interval` = sprintf("%.1f – %.1f", future$lower[future_steps, "95%"], future$upper[future_steps, "95%"]),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

Re-estimating on the full sample keeps the same model structure
(`r as.character(sarima_full)`) but updates the coefficients with the data up
to April 2025. The point forecast stays close to the recent level of the index,
around `r round(mean(future$mean[1:12]), 0)` index points over the next 12
months, while the 95% interval widens from
±`r round((future$upper[1, "95%"] - future$lower[1, "95%"]) / 2, 1)` points one
month ahead to about
±`r round((future$upper[h_future, "95%"] - future$lower[h_future, "95%"]) / 2, 0)`
points after three years.
